results.title: Using YAML Linters in Large Projects to Improve Code Quality and Consistency | MoldStud
results.content: # Best Practices for Using YAML Linters in Large Projects - Enhance Code Quality and Consistency. Explore key strategies for applying YAML linters in large projects to improve code clarity, reduce errors, and maintain consistent configurations across teams and environments. In sprawling environments where configuration files multiply rapidly, setting up these tools to enforce uniform style rules cuts debugging time drastically. For instance, `Pre-commit` integration supports multiple YAML linters, automating checks on every commit. Ultimately, the synergy between validators and development environments changes how teams work, reducing friction and improving clarity around YAML file structure. On the other hand, JavaScript ecosystems, especially those employing Node.js and React, can benefit from YAML validators integrated as ESLint plugins or through custom scripts that parse configuration files before runtime. Statistics from recent development surveys suggest that over 70% of teams using linters reported higher configuration inconsistencies when their linter lacked compatibility with the underlying platform. In my experience, teams that align linter capabilities with their stacks slash debug times and reduce configuration-related bugs by nearly 40%. According to a 2025 DevOps Institute report, teams embedding configuration linters within their CI saw a 35% reduction in rollout failures tied to environment misconfigurations. According to a 2025 survey by DevOps Digest, teams reducing syntax errors by standardizing configuration saw a 40% decrease in build failures. Keep configurations modular–use “extends” or “includes” features provided by linter tools to layer environment- or team-specific tweaks on top of the base rules, rather than rewriting from scratch. In practice, a unified linter config becomes the single source of truth, reducing debates around style and catching subtle YAML pitfalls upfront–especially handy as the project scales and contributors multiply. Integrate your preferred YAML syntax validator into the CI/CD workflow–for example, GitHub Actions or GitLab CI can run a linter step that validates all modified YAML files before merging. According to a 2025 survey by DevOps Institute, teams deploying pre-merge automated checks reduce configuration-related bugs by up to 40%. For example, integrating linting checks into the CI/CD pipeline reduces manual code reviews and reveals inconsistencies early, helping teams avoid costly reworks later in stages like food delivery app development services. YAML linters are essential tools for maintaining code quality in large projects.

results.title: Multifaceted intervention to reduce haemodialysis catheter related bloodstream infections: REDUCCTION stepped wedge, cluster randomised trial - PMC
results.content: Patients who require dialysis are among the groups at highest risk of healthcare associated infections.1 The use of central venous catheters as vascular access for haemodialysis adds to this risk through increasing the susceptibility to haemodialysis catheter related bloodstream infection (CRBSI), which is associated with higher morbidity, healthcare costs, and mortality.2 3 Because of the many elements of haemodialysis catheter care, multifaceted interventions, or care bundles, have been postulated as an effective means to reduce this infectious burden. Management of central venous catheters for haemodialysis (haemodialysis catheters) is complex and is perhaps best illustrated by the 20 topic areas in the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidelines for the prevention of intravascular catheter related infections.4 In such a context, care bundles, which usually contain three to five evidence informed interventions, offer an appealing approach to reduce unnecessary clinical variation and improve patient outcomes.5 6 The most prominent of the studies using this approach was the Michigan Keystone project, which found significant reductions (66%) in central venous CRBSIs using a before and after design in an intensive care setting.7 The evaluation of care bundles, however, both in general and in the specific setting of preventing central venous catheter related infections, has been limited by the paucity of evidence in a randomised setting. We designed a pragmatic, national, stepped wedge, cluster randomised trial (REDUcing the burden of dialysis Catheter ComplicaTIOns—a National approach (REDUCCTION)) to examine the effect of a multifaceted, evidence based, suite of interventions on CRBSI rates in renal services across Australia (box 1 lists the components of the suite). The primary outcome was analysed using a multilevel Poisson regression model to estimate the effect of treatment on infection rates, reported as incidence rate ratios with corresponding 95% confidence intervals for the comparative trial-wide rate at the service level of per 1000 catheter days of use between the baseline and intervention trial phases. In this large, national, cluster randomised trial, we tested the effect of implementing a care bundle comprised of evidence-based interventions used by treating renal services and found that the intervention did not reduce the rate of haemodialysis CRBSIs. The use of a randomised design allowed for a robust assessment of such a care bundle by adjusting for the effect of non-study related changes in practice that occur with time.

results.title: Interventions to improve the quality of low back pain care in emergency departments: a systematic review and meta-analysis | Internal and Emergency Medicine | Springer Nature Link
results.content:
Title: Interventions to improve the quality of low back pain care in emergency departments: a systematic review and meta-analysis | Internal and Emergency Medicine | Springer Nature Link
Since this review, additional studies have been published targeting other important aspects of ED LBP care including opioid prescribing and self-management education [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. Sixteen studies included participants with LBP-related leg symptoms [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. Health Serv Res 56(4):709–720")], eight studies evaluated clinician-targeted interventions [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. ISSN 0195-4210")], the intervention significantly reduced imaging rates (OR 0.60; 95% CI 0.39–0.93), whereas the effect was uncertain in the seven studies that reported low baseline imaging rates (i.e., < 36%) (OR 0.99; 95% CI 0.76–1.31) [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. ISSN 0195-4210")], the intervention reduced imaging rates (OR 0.65; 95% CI 0.45–0.94), whereas the effect was uncertain in the five studies that did not incorporate systems-based changes (OR 1.04; 95% CI 0.77–1.41) [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. There were only three studies that reported the number of participants who received a non-opioid medication in ED [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. Four of seven studies that reported the outcome of ED LOS presented data that could be pooled in meta-analysis (see online resource; Fig. S3) [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. Nine studies evaluated patient-level outcomes [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial. However, only half of the studies that reported lumbar imaging outcomes reported data that could be used in the meta-analysis, including only one cluster RCT [14 Effectiveness of a multifaceted intervention to improve emergency department care of low back pain: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial.

results.title: MegaLinter configuration Guide
results.content: MegaLinter configuration variables are defined in a .mega-linter.yml file at the root of the repository or with environment variables. You can see an example config file in this repo: .mega-linter.yml Configuration is assisted with autocompletion and validation in most commonly used IDEs, thanks to JSON schema stored on schemastore.org MegaLinter have all linters enabled by default, but allows to enable only some, or disable only some If you need to lint only a folder or exclude some files from linting, you can use optional environment parameters FILTER_REGEX_INCLUDE and FILTER_REGEX_EXCLUDE You can apply filters to a single linter by defining variable <LINTER_KEY>_FILTER_REGEX_INCLUDE and <LINTER_KEY>_FILTER_REGEX_EXCLUDE Warning: not applicable with linters using CLI lint mode project (see details) Mega-linter is able to apply fixes provided by linters. To use this capability, you need 3 env variables defined at top level Only for GitHub Action Workflow file if you use it: You may see github permission errors, or workflows not run on the new commit. See variables related to a single linter behavior in linters documentations MegaLinter can run custom commands before running linters (for example, installing an plugin required by one of the linters you use) Example in .mega-linter.yml config file MegaLinter can run custom commands after running linters (for example, running additional tests) Example in .mega-linter.yml config file MegaLinter runs on a docker image and calls the linters via command line to gather their results. As it can be complicated to trust the authors of all the open-source linters, MegaLinter removes variables from the environment used to call linters. You can add secured variables to the default list using configuration property SECURED_ENV_VARIABLES in .mega-linter.yml or in an environment variable (priority is given to ENV variables above .mega-linter.yml property). Example of adding extra secured variables .mega-linter.yml: Example of adding extra secured variables in CI variables, so they can not be overridden in .mega-linter.yml: Each linter has a lint mode by default, visible in its MegaLinter documentation (example): You can override the CLI_LINT_MODE by using configuration variable for each linter (see linters documentation) Allowing file or list_of_files to be overridden to project is mostly for workarounds, for example with linters that have a problem to find their config file when the current folder isn't the repo root.
